Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report



Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050




Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.
Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.

Instead, their projections highlight a predator-prey imbalance that could “fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems” in unforeseen ways, they said.
The seas around the British and Irish Isles, particularly the southern North Sea, have been identified as “marine climate hotspots”, one of 20 globally to have warmed the fastest over 50 years.
The new predictions, under a scenario of 3C (5.4F) of warming by 2100, found that while fish and seabed invertebrates may become more diverse by mid-century, key plankton groups lower in the food chain were likely to decline. This imbalance, the authors of the report said, could disrupt marine food webs and weaken the health and resilience of ocean ecosystems.
“What surprised us is that warming doesn’t increase or decrease biodiversity across the board,” said Elena Couce, a marine ecologist at the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas), a British government agency, and co-lead author of the study.
“While some groups higher up the food chain, like fish, may gain species in parts of the north-east Atlantic, key plankton groups that underpin marine ecosystems are projected to lose species,” she said.

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.raw_rss: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.raw_meta: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.jina_text:
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.




Image source, VCG via Getty Images
Image caption, 

This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra




August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.








'Burning with fever'




The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.









The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in Septembe

The vast majority of Australians support immigration and multiculturalism despite more feeling poorer – and increasingly pessimistic and distrustful of government, the annual Scanlon report on social cohesion has revealed.
People are more worried about artificial intelligence than climate change or going to war, but a global economic downturn and cost-of-living pressures are Australians’ key concerns.

Economic pain is also changing the way people vote, with people suffering hardship jumping ship to One Nation, according to the report, which is one of the country’s most extensive social research projects.

But, despite rising concern about antisemitism and Islamophobia, social cohesion in Australia has actually remained steady. The lead author of the report concedes many findings are cause for concern, but notes support for multiculturalism and diversity remains high, as does the sense of connection Australians feel to their communities.

The UK will assume the G20 presidency next year at a pivotal moment for international development and global cooperation. For Somalia, this presents an important opportunity to deepen a longstanding partnership with the UK and to ensure that the priorities of fragile and climate-vulnerable countries are reflected in the G20 agenda.
The UK has historically been a strong partner to Somalia, including on development, humanitarian response, climate finance, debt relief and institution building. But the context around this has changed significantly. Reduced foreign aid, alongside persistent geopolitical and climatic shocks, is creating new pressures for countries such as Somalia. We are seeking to consolidate hard-won gains and build sustainable economic resilience.
The UK’s focus on climate security is one that Somalia strongly shares. We have seen how recurrent droughts and floods can rapidly translate into food insecurity, displacement, fiscal pressures and humanitarian crises. And these challenges are not unique to Somalia. The UK’s G20 presidency provides an opportunity to put fragility at the heart of the debate on reforming the international financial architecture.




Somalia’s near decade-long debt relief process, which the UK championed, demonstrates that fragile states can deliver difficult reforms when there is national ownership, political continuity and sustained international support. But debt relief in 2023 did not remove Somalia’s underlying fragility. Why? Because the international financial architecture still does not adequately reflect the realities of fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS).
While all fragile states must rightly focus on fiscal sustainability, using domestic resources and undertaking structural reforms to their economies, they also need greater political and policy support to access the international financial architecture on terms that reflect their circumstances. This could be the real game changer.

Access to international finance, including climate finance, remains disproportionately difficult for fragile states. Complex accreditation, fiduciary and project requirements often favour countries with stronger institutions, creating what some have called a “fragility penalty” for countries most exposed to shocks like Somalia.

Funding to help poorer countries cope with climate crisis has stalled, says UN



Report reveals financial support promised by rich nations for adaptation measures is well behind the pace that is needed




Flows of money to help poor countries cope with the climate crisis have been flat or falling since 2022, despite growing impacts from extreme weather and warnings from scientists that global heating may be accelerating.
A new UN report has revealed that financial support for adaptation – which includes measures such as stronger infrastructure, early warning systems, flood protection and drought-resilient irrigation – is woefully short of what is needed and far behind even the inadequate promises that rich countries signed up to in 2021 in recognition of their far greater responsibility for the crisis.



View image in fullscreen
Flooding in Chattogram, Bangladesh, in July 2025. Photograph: Md Rafayat Haque Khan/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
The world’s 155 developing nations will need $305bn (£226bn) annually by 2035 to adapt to heatwaves, fires, floods, storms, droughts and rising sea levels that are made more intense or more frequent as a result of decades of burning fossil fuels, mostly in wealthy global north nations, according to the UN Environment Programme.
Yet finance flows from rich to poor countries were at most $32bn in 2024, the latest year for which data is available. That was only a billion up on the previous year, and down from the peak of 2022, partly because many governments in Europe are devoting more of their budgets to defence spending.


View image in fullscreen
Flood-damaged property in Devighat, Nepal, in September. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters
This is well behind the pace required to meet the goal of hitting $40bn by 2025, though some of the shortfall is expected to have been made up last year by multinational development banks, the report said.
At the Cop30 global climate talks in Belém, Brazil, last year, wealthy nations agreed to triple adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035. This increase to between $85bn and $120bn would reduce the gap, but still meet only 20-29% of needs, the report said.
The world’s least developed countries (LDCs) and small island states are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis and least able to pay for upgrades to infrastructure, such as more sea barriers and firefighting equipment. Researchers find the birds’ guano feeds algal blooms that absorb significantly more solar energy




Penguin poo is making the Antarctic snow melt faster, a study shows. As temperatures rise, penguins are waddling closer to the south pole, with potential for this previously unrecognised phenomenon to affect a wider area.
Snow algae are tiny single-celled plants that make a home in some of the coldest places on Earth. When nutrients are scarce, the algae produces red pigments to protect itself from the sun and slow growth.

And when nutrients are abundant, it proliferates, packing its cells with green chlorophyll to boost photosynthesis and grow. Snow containing green algae absorbs significantly more solar energy than snow containing red algae, making it melt more quickly.
Alia Khan from the University of Colorado and her team wanted to understand the impact of penguin poo on snow algae. They held their noses and gathered samples of red and green snow algae along the coast of the West Antarctic peninsula, in areas with and without penguin colonies.
Their results, published in Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences, showthat penguins track their poo, or guano, across snowfields, inadvertently feeding the algae and increasing green blooms, making the snow more likely to melt.
Projections of Antarctic melting do not yet take this phenomenon into account, but it could be significant, particularly as penguins move south.

The UK government has slashed overseas aid to Commonwealth countries, the Guardian can reveal, in contrast to the warm words for the group from King Charles and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, this week.
Amid sharp cuts in the UK’s aid budget overall, the Commonwealth has fared poorly, an analysis of the most recent and projected aid figures, seen by the Guardian, has shown.

Funding from the UK to the Commonwealth nations that previously had bilateral aid programmes will be cut from £546m in 2024-25 to £131m in 2028-29. Of that total, a large chunk – £68m – will go to Nigeria, leaving £63m for other countries.
The revelations come as the king attends the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) this week in Antigua, where he said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices” of slavery but where Burnham’s government fought to ensure that any discussion of reparations would be off the agenda.
The government has been cutting back on aid to countries that have been rapidly developing and are now judged to be middle income, such as India and Antigua, but the cuts to Commonwealth countries go much further, including many countries that are still among the poorest and many that are struggling under heavy debt burdens.
For example, Sierra Leone, one of the world’s least developed countries, will have its aid slashed from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. The UK and Sierra Leone will act as co-conveners of a strand of talks focusing on adaptation to the impacts of the climate crisis, at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey next week.
Aid to Rwanda, where the previous government had a scheme to send refugees, is also being cut from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. Aid to Tanzania will be slashed from £60m in 2025-26 to £5m in 2028-29. The Caribbean Development Team will have its funding cut from more than £98m in 2025-26 to £45m in 2026-27.

A spending watchdog has strongly criticised the lack of progress made by public sector organisations in tackling climate change.
Audit Wales says since a Welsh government "climate emergency" was declared in 2019, "decarbonisation" has become a lower priority for public bodies.
It says there are many examples of positive changes but the "collective ambition" for a net zero public sector in Wales by 2030 is unlikely to be met.
It has been estimated that it would cost at least £2.3bn to decarbonise Welsh council buildings alone.
The Welsh government said its 2030 ambition had "driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do".
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.







Wales 'to go further' on climate target





Wales facing unrecognisable future, warns commissioner














In its new report, the spending watchdog said public bodies in all sectors recognise decarbonisation is important.
But it said: "Since 2022, financial and political pressures have caused decarbonisation to fall down the priority list.
"Public bodies told us their overall financial pressures mean they are struggling to invest in decarbonisation."
It criticised the Welsh government for not defining the "collective ambition" for net zero by 2030 as a "target".
"There are also no penalties or incentives to drive compliance. Some public bodies told us this had added to uncertainty around the level of priority to attach to carbon reduction."
On spending, it added that public bodies had made "limited progress" overall in understanding how much it will cost to decarbonise in the near or longer term.
"Where public bodies have estimated the longer-term cost, some described it as unaffordable."
Ann-Marie Harkin from Audit Wales said: "We can list positive examples, but not enough progress has been made overall, and we owe it to future generations to do better."





In 2017, the then-Labour Welsh government called for a net zero public sector by 2030, saying that public bodies were "uniquely placed" to influence emissions in areas such as buildings and transport.
The thinking was that if government-backed bodies made the switch and invested in infrastructure like electric vehicles and charge points, renewable power and heating systems, it would make it easier and cheaper for the public to follow suit.
The "collective ambition" does not require every public body to reach net zero individually by 2030 but it is meant to provide a shared direction of travel and an expectation that all public bodies contribute towards reducing emissions.

Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing


Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations




Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area.
Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA.



View image in fullscreen
Boulders were loaded on to the Arctic Sunrise in Le Havre.  Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace
The Southern North Sea is an area of importance for harbour porpoises, supporting nearly 20% of the UK North Sea population. But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily.
Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said.





Greenpeace campaigners drop boulders onto the seabed to create anti-trawler barrier


“Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.”
The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks.





Greenpeace campaigner explains the “boulder barrier” on the seabed
The Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective.
“We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said.

Emily Beament

Environmentalists say they have deployed boulders weighing up to two tonnes each to prevent destructive fishing in an area of the sea created to protect porpoises.




It is the latest action by Greenpeace to prevent “bottom trawling” – a method of fishing in which gear is dragged across the seabed to scoop up fish – in the UK’s seas by dropping boulders to create an underwater barrier to the nets.








The environmental group deployed the boulders, to which celebrities Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch have added their names, over the weekend in the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area, which was designated to protect harbour porpoises.




Analysis shows that in 2025, bottom trawlers logged more than 37,000 fishing hours in the protected zone – far more than in any other offshore marine protected area, Greenpeace said.


Benedict Cumberbatch is among the celebrities to have added his name to a boulder in the latest direct action by Greenpeace (Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace/PA)





The campaigners warned that bottom trawling destroyed delicate seafloor habitats, depleted key fish stocks the porpoises rely on and disrupted their ability to hunt as a result of intense noise.




They claim to have effectively closed 116 square kilometres (44 square miles) of the marine protected area to bottom trawling in what they have declared as an “ocean park”.




And Greenpeace vessel the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter other types of destructive fishing over the coming days, the group said.











The latest deployment of boulders by Greenpeace – which has previously taken the same direct action in other parts of the UK seas – comes as Blue Planet III premiered on the BBC on Sunday.




Will McCallum, co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said:  “Blue Planet III powerfully shows us the majesty of our ocean – as well as the very grave threats it faces.







“Imagine a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park like Dartmoor or the Peak District.




“Out of sight, destruction on that scale is happening near our own shores in places we’re told are ‘Marine Protected Areas’.




“Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and seabirds.”


Greenpeace said the boulders had effectively shut off 116 square km of the marine protected area to bottom trawling (Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace/PA)

articles.jina_text:
Councillors have deferred a major planning application for 17 groynes after the RNLI made a formal objection to building of the groynes in April.
The charity previously claimed the council had ignored safety issues they had flagged, such as increased risk to tourists and rescue crews.
Blackpool Council has a statutory duty to deliver schemes to protect the coastline. It said if the proposals fall through, a new scheme would require a council contribution of £13m due to changes in government funding.




Image source, EPA
Image caption, 

Blackpool Council previously said beaches "could be lost" unless urgent action is taken




The proposed defences would see manmade rock headlands built on the beach to trap sand and prevent the loss of the town's sandy beaches. But since the application, more than 60 objections have been made.
But after the Blackpool beach management scheme was deferred by the council's planning committee last month, further discussions have been held regarding the risk assessments for the RNLI operations.
Since several multi-agency meetings and workshops have and are planned to discuss the risk assessment required by agencies for rescue and recovery operations around the groynes.
Blackpool Council's Health and Safety Teams have also assessed and updated the Council's Risk Assessments in respect of its own operations on the coastline. Subject to planning permission, work on the Bispham and Blackpool Beach Management schemes will start in early 2027.



'No longer funding'




But with government reductions in funding for new schemes announced this year, there is added pressure to ensure the current Blackpool Beach Management schemes can go ahead.
A report to Blackpool Council's Climate Change and Environmental Scrutiny Committee stated: "Consultation has taken place with business leaders all stakeholders and residents, which will continue throughout the pre-construction phase and once the schemes commence on site.
"If funding is withdrawn for these schemes there is no longer funding in the future at the current 100% level.
"New funding rules introduced by the Environment Agency in April 2026 require any new schemes to provide 10% of the capital funding for scheme over £3m in value.
"In the case of the Blackpool Beach Management schemes this would mean a contribution of £13m."

Officials in Boulder County, Colorado, say they have a safe plan to wipe out invasive weeds, but some locals are concerned




Soon, weed-killing chemicals will start falling from the sky over the Red Hill area of Boulder county, Colorado.
The wildland is known for its biodiversity, home to hundreds of important species and a concentration of rare environmental resources. It is a key habitat for beloved herds of elk and bighorn sheep, with farms and ranchland lying at its base.

But any day now, hundreds of acres of Red Hill are set to become the target for drone spraying of a chemical herbicide that some researchers warn come with concerns.
County officials say the plan is an effective and essential move that will wipe out invasive weeds and mitigate the risk of dangerous and costly wildfires that could use the unwanted vegetation as fuel.



They tout Boulder county as “ground zero” for research and testing of indaziflam - a relatively new herbicide developed by Bayer, the German chemical and pharmaceutical conglomerate, that has been approved for use across millions of acres of public lands as a tool for preserving native ecosystems.
But the drone spray project has prompted an outcry from many people living and working in the area as some scientists say the chemical comes with serious risks for vulnerable species and poses health dangers for people and animals, including through water that runs off the steep slope into rivers and creeks and into groundwater supplies for crop irrigation, though the chemical’s manufacturer denies that it is unsafe.
In June, two University of Colorado researchers added fuel to the community concerns, publishing a journal article highlighting risks to ecological and human health from indaziflam spraying and arguing that the cheatgrass issues cited as a basis for spraying are overblown. They cited prior published studies that raise concerns about genotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
“It really directly affects all residents downstream from this,” said Azuraye Wycoff, owner of Yellow Barn Farm, a regenerative agricultural operation tending to crops, sheep, pigs and other livestock located at the base of Red Hill. “There are a lot of people in our community who are really livid about it.”


Opponents fear the work could start this month.


View image in fullscreen
The weed killer indaziflam will be sprayed near Yellow Barn Farm. Photograph: Yellow Barn Farm
Adding to the worries is evidence that the indaziflam product to be used, sold under the brand name Rejuvra, contains per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (Pfas), a class of chemicals linked to a range of health risks and known to persist in the environment. There have been years of ongoing federal and state actions to rein in Pfas contamination.

Security experts fear the influx will gather pace following the Government’s decision to devolve more spending powers to councils, which are increasingly attracted to the lower cost of Chinese vehicles compared to Western counterparts.

Security fears over components in Chinese EVs have seen such vehicles banned by the Ministry of Defence over spying concerns, while the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) found it was “technically possible” for electric buses from China already on Britain’s roads to be remotely stopped by Beijing.

Security experts fear the influx will gather pace following the Government’s decision to devolve more spending powers to councils, which are increasingly attracted to the lower cost of Chinese vehicles compared to Western counterparts. 



Luke de Pulford, co-founder of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, said more regional spending decisions are likely to result in “an increasing amount of the purchasing of risky Chinese tech outsourced to councils”.





He said: “As we move towards a greener economy, there is heavy pressure on public authorities to procure green vehicles,” adding that lower prices will put “pressure upon local authorities to get them from Chinese sources”.



“We’ll be talking buses used to transport senior citizens and everybody else.”



Security fears over components in Chinese EVs have seen such vehicles banned by the Ministry of Defence over spying concerns, while the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) found it was “technically possible” for electric buses from China already on Britain’s roads to be remotely stopped by Beijing.

Security figures warn the risk could grow as devolved spending powers push cost-conscious councils toward cheaper, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles over Western alternatives.

articles.jina_text:
The UK Government wants to see the Acorn carbon capture and storage project succeed, a UK minister has said, after concerns were raised about the way it is being funded.




The project in Aberdeenshire was due to receive £200 million in grant funding from the UK Government, but Chancellor John Healey changed the commitment to mean the UK Government would offer the same amount in loans or receive an equity stake in the project.








Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney has said he was “deeply concerned” about changes to the funding mechanism.




Acorn, which could support about 15,000 jobs at its peak, proposes storing emissions from across Scotland under the seabed of the North Sea.


(PA Graphics)

UK Government energy minister Martin McCluskey said it had been necessary to “reprioritise” budgets to prioritise investing in defence, but that the UK Government wanted to support the project.




He told The Sunday Show on the BBC: “We awarded £200 million in grant funding at the last spending review.




“Some of that has already been drawn down by the developers, and the money that they’ve already drawn down remains in place.













“For the remainder, and for any future support, instead of it being through grant funding, it will be through loans and equities.




“Why are we doing that? We’re doing that for two reasons. Firstly, loans and equities are better value for the taxpayer. It means that perhaps we could choose to take a stake in that project, which would give a return to the taxpayer.









“But second, we’ve had to make some really difficult choices to reprioritise within budgets in order to fund the defence investment plan, which is obviously a priority for the Government.”




Mr McCluskey said the UK Government has had to “reprioritise” carbon capture and storage programmes right across the UK, and that a number of programmes have actually been stopped, not just reprioritised in terms of loans and equities.

Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.
Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies.

After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.
During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.

Announcing his plans, the chancellor said clean power is “how we break the grip of international gas prices on our bills”, but added the shift towards it “has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it”.

New offshore wind projects lodging bids for subsidy contracts will only get signed off by ministers if they believe that all the power generated could be accommodated by Britain’s electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers.

There is concern in government that wasted wind charges could add to energy bills, with the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is funded through energy bills, being forced to pay wind turbines to switch off when there is not sufficient cabling capacity to transmit their power to consumers.
A National Audit Office report in September warned that homes and businesses could be faced with a potential annual bill of £7.8bn by 2030 to deal with the issue.

Full SummaryA new report from the Helsinki-based think tank CREA reveals that wildfire smoke caused an estimated 3,560 deaths in Indonesia during September 2026, doubling the previous month's estimate. The worsening air quality, driven by forest and land fires, has significantly impacted public health and strained regional relations across Southeast Asia.
Smoke from Indonesia’s wildfires killed an estimated 3,560 people in September alone – twice the estimate for August – according to a new report.
The deaths from fire smoke made up about two thirds of the 5,310 deaths from all air pollution in Indonesia in September.
This marked a rise of 42 per cent from 3,740 in August, in a country of about 278 million people. 
A further 1,750 deaths came from urban and industrial pollution.





The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank, estimated the deaths from short-term exposure to fine particle pollution, known as PM2.5, in the days after exposure, and gave a range of 4,610 to 6,080 for the total. The figures are estimates and not a count of recorded deaths.

articles.jina_text:
John Swinney has said he is “deeply concerned” by the decision to cancel grant funding for an “absolutely central” carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility.




The Acorn project in Aberdeenshire was due to receive £200 million in grant funding from the UK Government, but Chancellor John Healey changed the commitment to mean the UK Government would offer the same amount in loans or receive an equity stake in the project.








UK ministers were accused of causing confusion over the funding this week, with Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds telling the BBC: “There hasn’t been a cut to the £200 million, I can reassure you that that commitment stands.




“That is the grant funding, but there could well be loans or equity stakes taken, because we will need probably additional funding to secure the future of this project.”




Speaking to the Press Association on Friday, the First Minister voiced his opposition to the decision.




“I raised the issue of Acorn and my concerns about the fact that I think further uncertainty has been created for Acorn,” he said.













“What I understand the position to be is the UK Government has decided not to offer grant funding to the Acorn project, but instead to do that through financial transactions.




“That creates more risk, that creates more uncertainty about the project.




“The very act of changing the funding mechanism does that, and I am deeply concerned about that because I think the Acorn project is an absolutely central project in relation to our work on climate action and it’s essential that it’s taken forward as part of that agenda and as part of encouraging the reindustrialisation of Scotland.”









A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said: “We recognise Acorn’s role in supporting good, well-paid jobs and reindustrialisation in Scotland.




“Acorn will continue to receive its existing grant funding until the end of the year.




“Future support will be through loans or equity stakes that need to see the taxpayer receive a return.

Andrea Egan calls for same political focus on teachers, care sector and NHS and says Jackdaw decision ‘a serious misstep’ 
 
 
UK politics live – latest updates  




The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.
Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said that too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.

“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”


North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.







Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners

Read more
The decision was met with anger by climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will drive the escalating crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year.
After Wednesday’s budget, the forecasts for which factored in the project’s approval, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs are lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decides to block Rosebank.
But Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. Instead, she said ministers should focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of people who work in the public sector which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.


“It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.”

articles.jina_text:
Londoners could face freezing temperatures far sooner than expected, as El Niño continues to strengthen across the Pacific to what some scientists are calling “unprecedented levels”.




Forecasters have warned that the global phenomenon could disrupt the polar vortex – a vast ring of freezing winds high above the Arctic that normally keeps the coldest air contained around the North Pole.








Should the vortex weaken, it could disrupt the jet stream, allowing bitterly cold Arctic air to plunge southwards towards Europe.




And the impact could be felt across the capital as early as November, with London facing a sudden drop in temperatures months earlier than previously expected.




It was initially anticipated that temperatures would drop in January of next year. 


Londoners could face freezing temperatures far sooner than expected this winter
PA Wire




But NASA forecasts show the wind circulation weakening, with wind strength falling to 26.9mph on October 31, to 20.5mph on November 1 and 9.3mph on November 3. 




The development has raised questions over what it could mean for winter in the UK, particularly as forecasters monitor the possibility of a sudden stratospheric warming event.








“The stratospheric sudden warming can sometimes cause the jet stream to ‘snake’ more, and this tends to create a large area of blocking high pressure,” the forecaster said.













Experts say this weather pattern typically develops over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia, bringing the prospect of prolonged periods of cold, dry weather across northern Europe, including the UK.




Meanwhile, southern parts of Europe are more likely to experience milder, wetter and windier conditions.


People in snowy conditions in Westminster central London
PA Wire




Along the boundary of these areas, easterly winds can develop, dragging colder air westwards. 




In some cases, the plunge in temperatures can bring snowfall as seen during the severe cold spell of early 2018, infamously known as the 'Beast from the East'.









But forecasters can only reliably predict sudden stratospheric warmings around a week in advance. 




The chances of an atmospheric disruption are unusually high this year. Meteorological models are currently tracking an imminent, potentially record-breaking event, with forecasting odds sitting between 61% and 86% for a major stratospheric disturbance.




Dr Judah Cohen, an atmospheric and environmental research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), told Fox Weather: “This will be, I think almost undoubtedly, the largest, earliest disruption of the polar vortex on record.”


London is set for a particularly wet and stormy winter as a result of El Nino
AFP/Getty




Government officials and emergency campaigns, such as the 'Be Ready' initiative, have urged households to stockpile a three-day to two-week supply of essential items to prepare for severe disruptions brought about by the extreme weather.

The phenomenon is expected to hit countries like Nigeria, India, and China the hardest, with researchers linking the increasing strength of El Niño events to human-caused climate change.
Super El Niño could lead to nearly 900,000 extra deaths worldwide over just 10 months, climate scientists have warned in an alarming new prediction. 
The El Niño Heat Mortality Tracker, produced by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, forecasts the human impact of the weather phenomenon. El Niño occurs when the average sea surface temperatures in the central and tropical Pacific Ocean rise above the long-term average by 2C or more.
Researchers estimate the climate pattern has already lead to 484,500 excess heat-related deaths between June and September this year, with around 372,900 more forecast for the next six months. 




The mortality tracker map gives a breakdown of which countries are most badly affected, with Nigeria expected to see the highest death toll. Experts predict the African nation will see more than 56,000 additional deaths across the next six months, according to Climate Impact Lab.
